# Evergreen Notes (LYT)

Evergreen notes are notes written to grow in value. [[Nick Milo]] credits the term to Andy Matuschak, as a digital evolution of the atomic notes of Niklas Luhmann. They are the output of [[Note-Making]].

## Properties
According to Milo, evergreen notes are:
- **Clear and concise**: the title is a clear phrase or statement, a mini-thesis that tends to keep the note atomic. Size follows a Goldilocks rule: if linking to it is hard because it says many things, it is too long.
- **In your own words**, which draws out your own view.
- **Linked** to other notes.
- **Non-static**: rewritten as you learn.

## Things and statements
Milo separates "things" (concepts, known facts, standards, definitions, people, places) from "statements" (opinions about things). Thing notes are sturdy dots; statement notes hang off them. For example a note on a document can link to a statement such as "no one is above the law". A healthy system needs both. In version 1.5 the kit reflected this by renaming a folder to Things and adding Statements.

## Why they pay off
- **Antifragile**: each link, even to a contradicting idea, adds perspective, so the note gains from stress.
- **Compounding**: value builds over time, like interest (see [[Incremental Knowledge Accumulation]] for a related idea in this wiki).
- **Reusable**: the same note can serve several efforts across years, though it costs more to write than an ordinary note.

## Not dogmatic
Milo says notes need not be tiny: over-fragmenting is its own form of over-structuring. Notes can be long or short, messy or clean, split or merged, and edited years later, and valuable ones should generally focus on one main idea.
